To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the patient’s gender, ethnicity and social class have a significant effect on the quality of the doctor-patient interaction, and that (ii) this effect is mediated by the doctor’s implicit attitudes towards these social groups.

the following factors were associated with a greater likelihood of receiving a prescription for opioids: (1) being female; (2) being white; (3) having a higher level of education; (4) having a higher annual household income; (5) living in a rural county; and (6) living in a county with a higher proportion of residents with a college degree.
The patient's social class, education level, and ethnicity have a significant impact on their medical care.

the role of prejudice in medicine, and the consequences of prejudice on health.
the role that doctors play in the creation of inequalities in health care.
how the social and cultural context of health care delivery shapes patients’ experiences, health outcomes, and the quality of care.

we are all prejudiced, and we all have implicit biases that we may not even know we have.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the patient’s race and the doctor’s race are both important predictors of the doctor’s treatment of the patient, and that both the patient’s race as well as the doctor’s race have independent effects.
the patient’s perception of the physician’s bias has a significant effect on patient health and health outcomes.
we need to be more aware of our own biases and prejudices, as they may affect our interactions with patients.
